title: A Claim Was Not Control Everywhere
definition: The actual ability to carry out authority in a place, rather than only claim it.
content:
A colonial authority could claim a territory without controlling every community within it. To investigate actual control, ask what happened in a particular place and period. Were instructions carried out? Was tribute collected? Who made decisions? A boundary drawn on a map does not answer all these questions. A single expedition also does not automatically establish lasting rule.

Our fictional source desk compares a map claim, an order and a record of a local action. The map shows what its maker represented. The order shows what an authority wanted. The action record may help investigate practice. Keep their dates and purposes separate. Do not turn one successful visit into permanent control of a whole region, or one failed action into proof that no contact ever occurred. This is a way to read evidence, not a map of present-day legal rights or instructions about modern government.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.
clues: Claim
A territorial claim states an asserted authority.
Practice
Effective control needs evidence of authority actually carried out.
Limit
One map or expedition does not establish lasting control of every community.
task: A shaded colonial map is used to claim every local order was obeyed. What is missing?
Evidence of authority actually carried out in particular communities
Only a darker map color
An assumption that every visit meant lasting rule
A rule that all communities had identical responses
reason: Evidence of authority actually carried out in particular communities. One map or expedition does not establish lasting control of every community.

title: Autonomy Meant Local Decisions
definition: The ability of a community to make and maintain decisions about its own affairs.
content:
Communities could maintain important decisions and institutions beyond effective Spanish rule. In this historical lesson, autonomy concerns local affairs and authority. It does not mean that everyone in a community had equal power, that no rules existed, or that the community had no connections with others. Ask which decisions people maintained and under what conditions.

A UCLA research summary of Stephen Acabado and Marlon Martins work describes Ifugao resistance to Spanish conquest alongside strategies for strengthening local organization. This is a named case, not every highland communitys identical history. Our modern clue card asks who made a decision and what evidence shows it being carried out. It is not a drawing of a universal council or a present-day legal definition of autonomous regions. More detailed Ifugao and other Cordillera histories follow later in the chapter.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.
clues: Local affairs
Autonomy concerns maintaining decisions about community affairs.
Named case
Ifugao research links resistance with local strategies and organization.
Scope
Autonomy is not equal power for everyone or the absence of rules and contacts.
task: A community maintained important local decisions. Which explanation fits historical autonomy?
Local decision-making could continue without unlimited freedom or equal power for everyone
No one had any rules
Every person had identical authority
The community could not interact with anyone
reason: Local decision-making could continue without unlimited freedom or equal power for everyone. Autonomy is not equal power for everyone or the absence of rules and contacts.

title: Contact Did Not Automatically Mean Conquest
definition: An interaction between people or groups.
content:
Communities could trade, negotiate or encounter colonial forces without every interaction producing complete colonial control. A treaty text records an agreement or claim, but its implementation needs evidence. A garrison is a military post; its presence in one place does not by itself establish identical authority throughout surrounding communities.

Najeeb Saleebys 1908 History of Sulu distinguishes Spanish claims and positions from limits on authority beyond them. The book also collects treaty texts and accounts of trade. Read it critically: it was written after Spanish rule in an American colonial setting and contains dated language and judgments. We use a limited example to ask about different forms of authority, not to repeat its stereotypes or decide present-day territorial disputes. A fuller account of Muslim polities and communities follows in Mission 2.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.
clues: Interactions
Trade and negotiation are forms of contact, not automatic proof of complete conquest.
Place matters
A post in one place does not establish the same authority everywhere around it.
Source limit
Treaty wording and an authors account need dated evidence of actual practice.
task: A military post in one location is used to claim identical control throughout a region. What should be checked?
Authority and local practice beyond that post
Only the posts name
An assumption that every interaction was conquest
A claim that no local institutions existed
reason: Authority and local practice beyond that post. Treaty wording and an authors account need dated evidence of actual practice.

title: Autonomy Did Not Mean an Unchanging Life
definition: Adjusting activities or arrangements in response to conditions.
content:
Resisting conquest did not require a community to remain unchanged. People could adjust livelihoods, organization and relationships while defending local authority. Terrain could affect movement and resources, but mountains alone do not explain peoples decisions or every colonial outcome. Keep the people and their actions in the explanation.

The UCLA account of Ifugao research describes people using economic opportunities and strengthening local organization. This challenges a picture of an isolated society frozen outside history. Our fictional comparison cards show a community keeping a local decision while changing an exchange activity. They illustrate a possible relationship, not a surviving transaction or proof of every persons motive. To explain actual change, use archaeological, documentary and community evidence for the named place and period. Change is not a measure of greater or lesser human worth.

Open the three clues and choose an explanation they support. Use Explain for help or revisit the lesson before targeted practice if the topic needs review.
clues: People act
Communities could adjust activities while maintaining local authority.
Connections
Economic interaction does not automatically erase autonomy.
No frozen history
Resistance does not prove isolation or unchanged practices across centuries.
task: A report says resisting conquest meant no changes or outside connections. What correction fits?
People could adapt and interact while defending local authority
All resistance required complete isolation
Mountains alone made every decision
Every community remained identical forever
reason: People could adapt and interact while defending local authority. Resistance does not prove isolation or unchanged practices across centuries.

title: Compare Claims with Community Evidence
definition: The standpoint and purpose from which a source presents information.
content:
A colonial report might call an area controlled while local evidence points to different limits. Do not assume that one official label is the complete story. Ask who produced each source, when, for what purpose and whose actions it records. Community knowledge and archaeological evidence can help investigate questions that an official report leaves out.

UCLA describes collaboration between researchers and descendant communities in interpreting Ifugao history. This is not permission to invent a single voice for every community member. Our fictional portfolio separates a map claim, a dated action record and a later community account. Match each to a question it can support, and identify gaps or disagreement. A modern account should keep its own date rather than be presented as an unchanged colonial statement. No student is asked to disclose ancestry, faith or family identity to complete the activity.

clues: Perspective
A source has a maker, purpose and setting.
Compare evidence
Official claims, community accounts and archaeology can answer different questions.
Respect limits

task: An official label and a community account differ. What should a historian do?
Compare their dates, purposes and evidence instead of treating one label as complete
Assume the official label records every local experience
Invent a compromise with no evidence
Treat the later account as an exact colonial quotation
reason: Compare their dates, purposes and evidence instead of treating one label as complete. No single source automatically speaks for every person or period.

title: Prepare Your Autonomy Evidence Report
definition: The standpoint and purpose from which a source presents information.
content: Review five ideas. A territorial claim was not proof of effective control everywhere. Autonomy concerned local decisions, not the absence of institutions. Trade, treaties and military posts required separate evidence about actual authority. Communities could change and interact while defending local affairs. Different sources and community knowledge help investigate limits. Prepare a fictional report for another Grade 5 learner. Name the people, place and period, explain the claim or recorded action, give a supporting clue and state a limit. Do not use one garrison as every communitys experience, mountains as the only explanation, or resistance as proof of complete isolation. Label the source cards as models, and keep historical questions separate from present-day legal claims. The main quiz has five questions and three correct passes. Review linked learning content before practice and a retry if needed. Complete all missions, then pass the chapter challenge to earn the chapter badge.
clues: Perspective
A source has a maker, purpose and setting.
Compare evidence
Official claims, community accounts and archaeology can answer different questions.
Respect limits
No single source automatically speaks for every person or period.
task: Which report best explains the limits of colonial control?
Compare claims with actual authority, local decisions and dated evidence
Use a map color as proof of every local outcome
Treat all contact as complete conquest
Describe every autonomous community as unchanged and isolated
reason: Explain particular claims, actual authority and community decisions through dated evidence, with limits and different perspectives.
